title: Oona and the Sneaky Marmot
markdown:
The wind in the High Peaks whispered secrets only the oldest stones remembered. Mule bells, tiny brass heartbeats, echoed between jagged ridges. When the moon visited, it gathered on the snow like spilled cream. This was Oona’s home: towering granite teeth, valleys that swooped like playful eagles. She had fingers as fleet as a fox, knotting with nimble notions, and a mind that could devise a contraption from moss and goat-hair. Her most treasured companion was Pudding, a goat kid with more spots than a starry night and a bleat that could curdle milk if he put his mind to it. Boundless energy. Surprising agility. Always underfoot. Always observing. Pudding knew the path.

One crisp morning a gust smelling of parchment and lavender blew a visitor to her doorstep: Professor Fitzwilliam Pumble, spectacles as thick as mountain ice, a beard that housed an ecosystem of forgotten crumbs. Quite lost, like a teacup dropped in a rockslide.

“My dear goblin,” he puffed, spectacles sliding. “I seem to have misplaced my bearings. I require a guide through these rather craggy environs. My map seems to have been eaten by a particularly enthusiastic weasel. A common occurrence, I assure you.”

Guide? Through these environs? She knew every lichen-covered rock and wobbly root, but a specific route was trickier. She mostly followed Pudding, who found the most interesting — and sometimes least dangerous — paths. Still, goblin ingenuity was her middle name. (Her first name was, of course, Oona.)

“A guide, you say?” A glint that promised adventure, or at least a good bit of fun. “Right this way, Professor. I know these mountains like the back of Pudding’s ear. And Pudding here — he’s practically a mountain goat himself.”

Pudding gave a confident maaaa and trotted ahead, hooves sure on stony ground. Promising. But the Goblin Council, ancient whiskered grumps in the deepest caves, insisted on proof of passage, proof of guidance. Who, in these lonely peaks, could witness that Oona had not merely wandered with the professor but actually guided him?

The answer, unfortunately, was Bartholomew. A particularly cantankerous marmot with a very specific habit: he liked to pop his head out just as something interesting was about to happen, and then vanish. Precisely when you needed him to say yes, she did guide him, Bartholomew would be nowhere. A witness with suspicious timing and a severe case of stage fright.

“Right then, Pudding. We’ll need Bartholomew to see us. Keep an extra sharp eye. For him, and for any wobbly bits.” Pudding twitched his ears, scanning the slopes. Pudding knew the path.

The path was steep, scree shifting like nervous cheese. Goblin smarts. Strong hands. Oona fashioned grips from twisted roots and goat-hair rope. Toggles clicked. Satisfyingly. Professor Pumble buried his nose in a tiny leather-bound notebook. “Fascinating fungal growth.” Oblivious to the sheer drop a few feet away.

When they reached a chasm spanned by a bridge that looked like well-chewed twigs held by hope and cobwebs, Pudding leaped first, testing each twig with a delicate hoof.

“Remarkable,” exclaimed the Professor. “The inherent buoyancy of these local flora. A new theory on arboreal suspension.”

Oona winked at Pudding, who chewed a stray piece of mountain grass.

Bartholomew played hide-and-seek. Just as a rogue gust threatened the Professor’s spectacular feathered hat, Oona spotted a flash of brown. “Bartholomew. See this. We’re helping the Professor. He needs his hat.” A whiskered face poked from behind a mossy rock, twitched, sniffed — poof — gone.

“He saw,” Oona declared. “He saw you nearly lose your hat, and me holding on tight. Evidence.” The Professor nodded absently, already sketching lichen.

Dusk painted apricot and plum. Near a magnificent waterfall — thunderous by day — the rising moon caught the spray. For a breathtaking moment the cascade became a river of liquid silver. Heart-aching beautiful.

“Oh, my stars and garters,” gasped the Professor, notebook clattering.

There, on a rocky outcrop, sat Bartholomew, little eyes wide, reflecting silver, mesmerized.

“You saw it. Proof. You saw me bringing the Professor safely.”

But Bartholomew had had enough of witnessing. Flick of fluffy tail. Vanished. Then he popped out. Then in. Then vanished again. Oona sighed. Honestly.

They continued, the silver memory a shared secret between Oona and Pudding. They navigated by stars, goblin instincts accurate especially when Pudding nudged. Pudding knew the path. At last they descended into a nestled village: cozy lights, baking bread, warmth. They had made it.

Professor Pumble thanked her, eyes shining, and hurried off to tell of fungal growths and silver waterfalls. Oona and Pudding leaned against a warm stone wall, tired and triumphant. Then a high-pitched whistle, like a tiny mountain breeze. Peeking from a haystack: Bartholomew. He scurried, chattered, nose twitching, and with a surprisingly clear gesture pointed a little paw at Oona, then at the path they’d come from. She did it. She guided him. And look what we saw.

Villagers emerged. They understood. Soon there was shared laughter, mugs of steaming berry juice that tasted like sunshine, and Oona’s Goblin Bread — fermented roots, a dash of optimism, an extra sprinkle of goblin magic. She shared with Pudding, who gobbled. She even offered a crumb to a surprisingly agreeable Bartholomew, who accepted with a dignified nod. The mule bells, somewhere up-ridge, kept their tiny brass heartbeat. Pudding knew the path. And for once, so did the marmot.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
